rationale:
Split into four independent children. Each is one substantive step of the supplied proof, stated as a general reusable lemma, and the four sit in separate Mathlib API areas:
- left_inverse_projection = step 1 (A := L⁻¹∘p, with A∘L = id and L∘A = p of norm ≤ 1).
- local_inverse = step 2 (inverse function theorem with a C¹ inverse k on an open set O), plus Dk(h(v₀)) = id, used in step 3. It also makes explicit the restriction to the region where Dh is invertible, which the C¹-on-O claim needs.
- chart_image_nhds = step 4 (properness gives N ∩ B_ρ(x) ⊆ ψ(V₀), the only consequence step 5 uses).
- lipschitz_near_point = step 7 (continuity of Dπ plus the mean value inequality, for any f that is C¹ on the ball with ‖Df(x)‖ ≤ c).

Parent glue, following the supplied steps:
1. Take the chart (V, W, ψ) at x and v₀ with ψ(v₀) = x; ψ is C¹ on V. Apply left_inverse_projection to L := Dψ(v₀), which is injective by the contract, to get A.
2. h := A(ψ − x) is C¹ on V with Dh(v₀) = A∘L = id. Apply local_inverse to get V₀, O, k. Then h(v₀) = 0 ∈ O, k(0) = v₀ and Dk(0) = id.
3. Apply chart_image_nhds (ψ is continuous on V) to get ρ.
4. Choose r₀ with B_{r₀}(0) ⊆ O, set δ := min(ρ, r₀/(‖A‖+1)) and π(y) := ψ(k(A(y − x))). Values of π off B_δ(x) are irrelevant to the frozen type.
5. (i) follows by ContDiffOn.comp, since A(y − x) ∈ B_{r₀}(0) ⊆ O.
6. (ii) holds because k(O) ⊆ V₀ ⊆ V and ψ(V) = W ∩ N.
7. (iii): y ∈ N ∩ B_δ(x) gives y = ψ(v) with v ∈ V₀, so π(y) = ψ(k(h(v))) = y.
8. (iv): the chain rule gives Dπ(x) = L∘id∘A = L∘A, of norm ≤ 1; then apply lipschitz_near_point with c = 1.

subproblems.title: A C¹ map is (c + η)-Lipschitz on small balls around a point where ‖Df‖ ≤ c
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, f : ℝ^P → ℝ^P, x ∈ ℝ^P and δ, c ∈ ℝ with δ > 0. Suppose f is C¹ on the open ball B_δ(x) and its Fréchet derivative at x (Mathlib fderiv ℝ f x) has operator norm ‖Df(x)‖ ≤ c. Then for every η > 0 there is s with 0 < s ≤ δ such that |f(y) − f(z)| ≤ (c + η)|y − z| for all y, z ∈ B_s(x).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (f : Euclid P → Euclid P) (x : Euclid P) (δ c : ℝ), 0 < δ → ContDiffOn ℝ 1 f (ball x δ) → ‖fderiv ℝ f x‖ ≤ c → ∀ η : ℝ, 0 < η → ∃ s : ℝ, 0 < s ∧ s ≤ δ ∧ ∀ y ∈ ball x s, ∀ z ∈ ball x s, ‖f y - f z‖ ≤ (c + η) * ‖y - z‖
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 7 of the parent proof (continuity of Dπ at x and the mean value inequality), stated for an arbitrary map f that is C¹ on the ball and an arbitrary bound c in place of π and ‖Dπ(x)‖ ≤ 1. No dependencies.
1. (Differentiability and continuity of the derivative on the ball.) The ball B_δ(x) is open and f is C¹ on it. Hence f is differentiable within B_δ(x) at each y ∈ B_δ(x) (C¹ implies differentiable; Mathlib ContDiffOn.differentiableOn with 1 ≠ 0), and since B_δ(x) is a neighbourhood of each of its points, f is differentiable at y with derivative Df(y) = fderiv ℝ f y (DifferentiableWithinAt.differentiableAt). Moreover y ↦ Df(y) is continuous on B_δ(x), because a C¹ function on an open set has continuous derivative there (ContDiffOn.continuousOn_fderiv_of_isOpen with 1 ≤ 1).
2. (Choice of s.) Since δ > 0, x ∈ B_δ(x), and as B_δ(x) is open, the continuity of y ↦ Df(y) on B_δ(x) gives continuity at x. Let η > 0. By continuity at x choose s₁ > 0 such that ‖Df(y) − Df(x)‖ < η for every y with |y − x| < s₁ (Metric.continuousAt_iff). Put s := min(s₁, δ). Then s > 0 and s ≤ δ.
3. (Derivative bound on B_s(x).) Let y ∈ B_s(x). Since |y − x| < s ≤ s₁, ‖Df(y) − Df(x)‖ < η, so by the triangle inequality for the operator norm ‖Df(y)‖ = ‖Df(x) + (Df(y) − Df(x))‖ ≤ ‖Df(x)‖ + ‖Df(y) − Df(x)‖ ≤ c + η. Since B_s(x) ⊆ B_δ(x), f is differentiable at y by step 1.
4. (Mean value inequality.) The ball B_s(x) is convex. By step 3, f is differentiable at every point of B_s(x) and ‖Df‖ ≤ c + η on B_s(x). The mean value inequality on convex sets says: if f is differentiable at every point of a convex set S and ‖Df‖ ≤ C on S, then |f(y) − f(z)| ≤ C|y − z| for all y, z ∈ S (Mathlib Convex.norm_image_sub_le_of_norm_fderiv_le). Applied with S = B_s(x) and C = c + η, it gives |f(y) − f(z)| ≤ (c + η)|y − z| for all y, z ∈ B_s(x).
5. Steps 2 and 4 give, for the arbitrary η > 0, a number s with 0 < s ≤ δ and the required inequality. ∎
proof_key_steps: C¹ on the open ball B_δ(x): f is differentiable at each point of the ball and y ↦ Df(y) is continuous there.
Continuity of Df at x gives s₁ > 0 with ‖Df(y) − Df(x)‖ < η for |y − x| < s₁; take s := min(s₁, δ).
Triangle inequality: ‖Df(y)‖ ≤ ‖Df(x)‖ + η ≤ c + η on B_s(x).
Mean value inequality on the convex ball B_s(x) gives |f(y) − f(z)| ≤ (c + η)|y − z|.

subproblems.title: Left inverse A of an injective linear map L with ‖L∘A‖ ≤ 1
subproblems.statement: Let P, d ∈ ℕ and let L : ℝ^d → ℝ^P be an injective continuous linear map. Then there is a continuous linear map A : ℝ^P → ℝ^d such that A∘L = id_{ℝ^d} and the operator norm of L∘A : ℝ^P → ℝ^P satisfies ‖L∘A‖ ≤ 1.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P d : ℕ) (L : Euclid d →L[ℝ] Euclid P), Injective L → ∃ A : Euclid P →L[ℝ] Euclid d, A.comp L = ContinuousLinearMap.id ℝ (Euclid d) ∧ ‖L.comp A‖ ≤ 1
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 1 of the parent proof (Q := L(ℝ^d), p the orthogonal projection onto Q with ‖p‖ ≤ 1 and p(Lw) = Lw, A := L⁻¹∘p), together with the identity L∘A = p used in step 7. No dependencies.
1. (The range and its orthogonal projection.) Let Q := L(ℝ^d) (Mathlib LinearMap.range L), a linear subspace of ℝ^P. Q is finite-dimensional, hence complete, so the orthogonal projection p : ℝ^P → Q onto Q exists (Submodule.orthogonalProjectionOnto Q). It is continuous and linear, and p(q) = q for every q ∈ Q (Submodule.orthogonalProjectionOnto_mem_subspace_eq_self). Let ι : Q → ℝ^P be the inclusion. The composite ι∘p : ℝ^P → ℝ^P is the orthogonal projection of ℝ^P onto Q regarded as an endomorphism of ℝ^P (Q.starProjection, which is by definition Q.subtypeL ∘ Q.orthogonalProjectionOnto). Its operator norm is at most 1 (Submodule.starProjection_norm_le; indeed y = ι(p(y)) + (y − ι(p(y))) with orthogonal summands, so |ι(p(y))| ≤ |y|).
2. (L is an isomorphism onto Q.) Since L is injective, e : ℝ^d → Q, e(w) := L(w), is a linear bijection (LinearEquiv.ofInjective), and ι(e(w)) = L(w) for all w ∈ ℝ^d. Because ℝ^d and Q are finite-dimensional, e and its inverse e⁻¹ : Q → ℝ^d are continuous (LinearEquiv.toContinuousLinearEquiv).
3. (Definition of A.) Let A := e⁻¹∘p : ℝ^P → ℝ^d. It is a composite of continuous linear maps, hence continuous linear.
4. (A∘L = id.) Let w ∈ ℝ^d. Then L(w) ∈ Q, so p(L(w)) = L(w), i.e. p(L(w)) is the element e(w) of Q. Therefore A(L(w)) = e⁻¹(e(w)) = w. As w is arbitrary, A∘L = id_{ℝ^d} as continuous linear maps.
5. (L∘A = ι∘p.) Let y ∈ ℝ^P. Then L(A(y)) = ι(e(A(y))) = ι(e(e⁻¹(p(y)))) = ι(p(y)). Hence L∘A = ι∘p = Q.starProjection.
6. (Norm bound.) By steps 5 and 1, ‖L∘A‖ = ‖ι∘p‖ ≤ 1. Steps 3, 4 and 6 prove the claim. (For d = 0 the argument is unchanged: Q = {0}, A = 0 and L∘A = 0.) ∎
proof_key_steps: Q := range L is finite-dimensional, so the orthogonal projection p : ℝ^P → Q exists, fixes Q, and ι∘p has operator norm ≤ 1.
Injectivity makes e : ℝ^d → Q, w ↦ Lw, a linear isomorphism with continuous inverse.
A := e⁻¹∘p satisfies A(Lw) = e⁻¹(e w) = w, so A∘L = id.
L∘A = ι∘p is the orthogonal projection onto Q, so ‖L∘A‖ ≤ 1.

subproblems.title: Inverse function theorem with a C¹ inverse on an open neighbourhood
subproblems.statement: Let d ∈ ℕ, h : ℝ^d → ℝ^d, V ⊆ ℝ^d open and v₀ ∈ V. Suppose h is C¹ on V and its Fréchet derivative at v₀ is the identity, Dh(v₀) = id_{ℝ^d}. Then there are open sets V₀, O ⊆ ℝ^d and a map k : ℝ^d → ℝ^d such that V₀ ⊆ V, v₀ ∈ V₀, h(V₀) ⊆ O, k(O) ⊆ V₀, k(h(v)) = v for all v ∈ V₀, h(k(u)) = u for all u ∈ O, k is C¹ on O, and the Fréchet derivative of k at h(v₀) is the identity.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (d : ℕ) (h : Euclid d → Euclid d) (V : Set (Euclid d)) (v₀ : Euclid d), IsOpen V → v₀ ∈ V → ContDiffOn ℝ 1 h V → fderiv ℝ h v₀ = ContinuousLinearMap.id ℝ (Euclid d) → ∃ (V₀ O : Set (Euclid d)) (k : Euclid d → Euclid d), IsOpen V₀ ∧ IsOpen O ∧ V₀ ⊆ V ∧ v₀ ∈ V₀ ∧ MapsTo h V₀ O ∧ MapsTo k O V₀ ∧ (∀ v ∈ V₀, k (h v) = v) ∧ (∀ u ∈ O, h (k u) = u) ∧ ContDiffOn ℝ 1 k O ∧ fderiv ℝ k (h v₀) = ContinuousLinearMap.id ℝ (Euclid d)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 2 of the parent proof (inverse function theorem for h := A(ψ − x) at v₀, giving open V₀ ⊆ V, O and the C¹ inverse k : O → V₀), together with Dk(h(v₀)) = Dh(v₀)⁻¹ = id, used in step 3. Only C¹ regularity of h is needed. No dependencies.
1. (Regularity of h.) V is open and h is C¹ on V, so h is C¹ at every v ∈ V (ContDiffOn.contDiffAt), in particular differentiable at v. The derivative map v ↦ Dh(v) is continuous on V (ContDiffOn.continuousOn_fderiv_of_isOpen). At v₀, Dh(v₀) = id is the underlying map of the identity continuous linear equivalence, so h has that equivalence as derivative at v₀; since h is C¹ at v₀, this derivative is strict (ContDiffAt.hasStrictFDerivAt').
2. (Inverse function theorem.) By the inverse function theorem (Mathlib HasStrictFDerivAt.toOpenPartialHomeomorph) there is a partial homeomorphism e of ℝ^d whose underlying function is h, with open source S, open target T and v₀ ∈ S (HasStrictFDerivAt.mem_toOpenPartialHomeomorph_source). Let g : ℝ^d → ℝ^d be its inverse function (e.symm). Then h(S) ⊆ T, g(T) ⊆ S, g(h(v)) = v for v ∈ S, h(g(u)) = u for u ∈ T, and g is continuous on T. Moreover g is by definition the local inverse of h at v₀, and it has strict, hence ordinary, derivative id⁻¹ = id at h(v₀) (HasStrictFDerivAt.to_localInverse).
3. (Where Dh is invertible.) Let G := {v ∈ V : ‖Dh(v) − id‖ < 1}. G is open: it is the intersection of the open set V with the preimage of the open unit ball around id under v ↦ Dh(v), which is continuous on V (ContinuousOn.isOpen_inter_preimage). Also v₀ ∈ G, because Dh(v₀) = id. For v ∈ G, Dh(v) is invertible. In the complete normed algebra of continuous linear endomorphisms of ℝ^d, any T with ‖T − 1‖ < 1 is a unit: T = 1 − (1 − T) with ‖1 − T‖ < 1, and the Neumann series Σₙ (1 − T)ⁿ converges to its inverse (Mathlib nonunits.subset_compl_ball). A unit U of this algebra is the underlying map of a continuous linear equivalence (ContinuousLinearEquiv.unitsEquiv).
4. (Definition of V₀, O, k.) Put V₀ := S ∩ G, O := {u ∈ T : g(u) ∈ V₀} and k := g. V₀ is open (S and G are open), V₀ ⊆ G ⊆ V, and v₀ ∈ V₀ by steps 2 and 3. O is open because g is continuous on the open set T and V₀ is open (OpenPartialHomeomorph.isOpen_inter_preimage_symm).
5. (Mapping and inverse identities.) Let v ∈ V₀. Then v ∈ S, so h(v) ∈ T and k(h(v)) = g(h(v)) = v ∈ V₀; hence h(v) ∈ O and k(h(v)) = v. Let u ∈ O. Then k(u) = g(u) ∈ V₀ by the definition of O, and h(k(u)) = u because u ∈ T. Thus h(V₀) ⊆ O, k(O) ⊆ V₀, k∘h = id on V₀ and h∘k = id on O.
6. (k is C¹ on O.) Let u ∈ O and a := k(u) ∈ V₀. Then a ∈ V, so h is C¹ at a (step 1), and a ∈ G, so Dh(a) is the underlying map of a continuous linear equivalence (step 3). Thus h has an invertible derivative at a = g(u), and u ∈ T. The C¹ inverse rule for partial homeomorphisms (Mathlib OpenPartialHomeomorph.contDiffAt_symm) says: if u lies in the target, the function has a continuous linear equivalence as derivative at g(u) and is Cⁿ at g(u), then the inverse g is Cⁿ at u. Hence k = g is C¹ at u. So k is C¹ at every point of O, hence C¹ on O.
7. (Derivative at h(v₀).) By step 2, k = g is differentiable at h(v₀) with derivative id, so Dk(h(v₀)) = id. Steps 4–7 give all the asserted properties. (The case d = 0 needs no change.) ∎
proof_key_steps: C¹ on the open set V: h is C¹ at each point of V, Dh is continuous on V, and h has strict derivative id at v₀.
Inverse function theorem: a partial homeomorphism e = h with open source S ∋ v₀ and open target T; its inverse g has derivative id at h(v₀).
G := {v ∈ V : ‖Dh(v) − id‖ < 1} is open, contains v₀, and Dh(v) is invertible for v ∈ G (Neumann series).
V₀ := S ∩ G, O := T ∩ g⁻¹(V₀) and k := g satisfy the mapping and two-sided inverse identities.
The C¹ inverse rule at each u ∈ O makes k C¹ on O, and Dk(h(v₀)) = id.

subproblems.title: Properness makes the chart image of an open parameter set a neighbourhood of ψ(v₀) in N
subproblems.statement: Let P, d ∈ ℕ, N, W ⊆ ℝ^P, V, V₀ ⊆ ℝ^d, ψ : ℝ^d → ℝ^P and v₀ ∈ ℝ^d. Suppose W is open, ψ is continuous on V and injective on V, ψ(V) = W ∩ N, V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact for every compact K ⊆ W, V₀ is open, V₀ ⊆ V and v₀ ∈ V₀. Then there is ρ > 0 such that N ∩ B_ρ(ψ(v₀)) ⊆ ψ(V₀).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P d : ℕ) (N W : Set (Euclid P)) (V V₀ : Set (Euclid d)) (ψ : Euclid d → Euclid P) (v₀ : Euclid d), IsOpen W → ContinuousOn ψ V → InjOn ψ V → ψ '' V = W ∩ N → (∀ K ⊆ W, IsCompact K → IsCompact (V ∩ ψ ⁻¹' K)) → IsOpen V₀ → V₀ ⊆ V → v₀ ∈ V₀ → ∃ ρ : ℝ, 0 < ρ ∧ N ∩ ball (ψ v₀) ρ ⊆ ψ '' V₀
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: step 4 of the parent proof. There, with F := V ∖ V₀, ψ(F) is relatively closed in W, so W₀ := W ∖ ψ(F) is an open neighbourhood of x = ψ(v₀) with W₀ ∩ N = ψ(V₀), and B_δ(x) ⊆ W₀ for small δ. Here the same compactness argument is run at the single point x as a proof by contradiction, which is all the parent uses. Continuity of ψ on V is the only regularity needed. No dependencies.
1. (x lies in W.) Put x := ψ(v₀). Since v₀ ∈ V₀ ⊆ V, x ∈ ψ(V) = W ∩ N, so x ∈ W. As W is open, choose r_W > 0 with B_{r_W}(x) ⊆ W.
2. (Contradiction hypothesis and a sequence.) Suppose that no ρ > 0 satisfies N ∩ B_ρ(x) ⊆ ψ(V₀). For every i ∈ ℕ, apply this to ρ_i := min(r_W, 1/(i+1)) > 0: there is y_i ∈ N with |y_i − x| < ρ_i and y_i ∉ ψ(V₀). Then y_i ∈ B_{r_W}(x) ⊆ W and |y_i − x| < 1/(i+1). So y_i → x as i → ∞: given ε > 0, pick i₀ with 1/(i₀+1) < ε; then |y_i − x| < 1/(i+1) ≤ 1/(i₀+1) < ε for i ≥ i₀.
3. (Preimages outside V₀.) For each i, y_i ∈ W ∩ N = ψ(V), so choose f_i ∈ V with ψ(f_i) = y_i. Then f_i ∉ V₀, for otherwise y_i = ψ(f_i) ∈ ψ(V₀).
4. (A compact set in W.) Let K := {x} ∪ {y_i : i ∈ ℕ}. K is compact, being a convergent sequence together with its limit (Mathlib Filter.Tendsto.isCompact_insert_range), and K ⊆ W because x ∈ W (step 1) and every y_i ∈ W (step 2). By the properness hypothesis, V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact. It contains every f_i, since f_i ∈ V and ψ(f_i) = y_i ∈ K.
5. (Convergent subsequence.) Compact subsets of ℝ^d are sequentially compact (IsCompact.tendsto_subseq). So there are a ∈ V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) and a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ with f_{φ(i)} → a. In particular a ∈ V.
6. (a ∉ V₀.) The complement ℝ^d ∖ V₀ is closed because V₀ is open, and it contains every f_{φ(i)} (step 3). Hence it contains the limit a, i.e. a ∉ V₀.
7. (ψ(a) = x.) ψ is continuous within V at a ∈ V, and f_{φ(i)} ∈ V with f_{φ(i)} → a, so ψ(f_{φ(i)}) → ψ(a). On the other hand ψ(f_{φ(i)}) = y_{φ(i)} → x, being a subsequence of the convergent sequence (y_i) (φ is strictly increasing, so φ(i) → ∞). Limits in ℝ^P are unique, so ψ(a) = x = ψ(v₀).
8. (Contradiction.) a ∈ V, v₀ ∈ V and ψ is injective on V, so a = v₀ ∈ V₀, contradicting step 6. Hence the assumption of step 2 is false, and there is ρ > 0 with N ∩ B_ρ(ψ(v₀)) ⊆ ψ(V₀). ∎
proof_key_steps: x := ψ(v₀) ∈ W; fix r_W > 0 with B_{r_W}(x) ⊆ W.
If no ρ works, pick y_i ∈ N ∩ B_{min(r_W, 1/(i+1))}(x) ∖ ψ(V₀); then y_i → x and y_i = ψ(f_i) with f_i ∈ V ∖ V₀.
K := {x} ∪ {y_i} is a compact subset of W, so the f_i lie in the compact set V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) and a subsequence converges to some a ∈ V.
a ∉ V₀ because the complement of V₀ is closed; ψ(a) = x by continuity of ψ on V and uniqueness of limits.
Injectivity of ψ on V gives a = v₀ ∈ V₀, a contradiction.
